papers.title: Somnus, a tunable, open-source platform for automated EEG sleep scoring in physiological and disease mouse models.
papers.abstract: Many studies using mouse models of human brain disorders rely on extended recordings of brain electrical activity through electroencephalogram, or EEG. The features that researchers measure in these recordings, such as seizures and epileptiform activity, are deeply influenced by whether the animal is awake, in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, or in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Because total sleep duration varies naturally across animals, rigorous experimental comparisons require classifying the sleep state of every few seconds of a recording. Manual annotation is highly labor-intensive, often requiring hours per subject. While automated scoring tools accelerate this process, they are typically trained exclusively on healthy cohorts and frequently fail when applied to disease models that exhibit atypical or fragmented sleep architecture. Somnus is an open-source Python package designed to automate rodent sleep staging using EEG, muscle activity (EMG), and optional video-tracking data. It includes a robust base model trained on diverse recordings from six independent laboratories, enabling out-of-the-box classification across various equipment setups without requiring prior manual labeling. A central feature of Somnus is its capacity for rapid adaptation to pathological sleep structure. The software provides a graphical interface that directs researchers to the specific epochs where the base model is least certain. Users can manually correct these targeted epochs in a built-in viewer by comparing the model's classification to the raw EEG signal and video, and then use their corrections to fine-tune the model. This workflow empowers researchers to generate accurate custom scorers for complex disease models or novel treatments with just a few minutes of manual correction, bypassing the need to hand-score entire experimental cohorts or develop their own models from scratch.

papers.title: Effectiveness of Rotating Versus Fixed Three-Section Watchkeeping Schedules on Crews' Well-Being, Cognitive Performance, Sleep and Salivary Cortisol in the Navy.
papers.abstract: When 24 h-work needs to be distributed among crew members on ships, on-watch duty times can be either stable over time or can vary on a regular basis. Research suggests that adaptation to permanent night shift might be less disruptive to humans' innate circadian rhythms than rotating schedules when external and social influences are minimized, such as when working on ships. Since the research on the question of rotation in the design of watchkeeping schedules is still not conclusively answered, the present research investigated the effects of a fixed and a daily rotating three-section watchkeeping schedule on crew members' vigilance performance, well-being, salivary cortisol and sleep quantity and continuity in five underways on board a German frigate. Results revealed better vigilance performance, less acute disruptions in salivary cortisol and less subjective sleepiness in the rotating watchkeeping schedule, especially for the night watch (watch on duty from 00 to 04). In contrast, sleep continuity was better in the fixed watchkeeping schedule. In sum, results favour rotating three-section watchkeeping schedules for cognitive functioning and well-being, but also suggest fixed three-section watchkeeping schedules are more suitable to maintain restorative sleep.

papers.title: Associations of the Low Arousal Threshold With Arrhythmia Burden and Heart Rate Variability in Obstructive Sleep Apnea Using Polysomnography With 24-h Holter Electrocardiography.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a widespread condition that increases the risk of arrhythmias. Recently, the role of specific OSA phenotypes, including the low respiratory arousal threshold (ArTH) phenotype, has been largely explored. This study aimed to assess whether the estimated low ArTH in patients with obstructive sleep apnea is significantly associated with arrhythmia burden and alterations in heart rate variability (HRV). Data from adults who underwent full-night video-polysomnography (vPSG) with 24-h 12-lead Holter electrocardiography (ECG) were included. ArTH was estimated noninvasively using the Edwards method. Arrhythmias were scored and counted. HRV was quantified in time, geometric, and frequency domains using ECG across a predefined circadian schedule. The analysis included 166 participants; 134 were classified as low ArTH, and 32 as high ArTH. The low ArTH group had a lower supraventricular arrhythmia burden, including fewer supraventricular premature contractions (SVPC), fewer SVPC pairs, and fewer supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) episodes than the high ArTH group. Daytime HRV differed between the groups, with higher RMSSD in low ArTH and higher LF power. In multivariable analyses, low ArTH remained associated with SVPC and SVPC pairs. Differences in HRV parameters were limited and were largely attenuated after adjustment for clinical confounders. The results suggest the potential importance of the ArTH phenotype as an independent indicator of arrhythmia in patients with OSA. However, the results should be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis gathering. Further, prospective studies are needed to assess the utility of ArTH in risk stratification.

papers.title: Assessing non-invasive glymphatic MRI markers following short-term sleep loss.
papers.abstract: The glymphatic system is a sleep-active pathway involved in clearing metabolic waste from the brain. Several non-invasive MRI indices have been proposed as proxies for assessing glymphatic function in vivo . However, it remains unclear whether these indices capture glymphatic dysregulation under short-term sleep loss. Using a large ENIGMA-sleep intervention dataset (n = 429) spanning ten international sites, we examined choroid plexus volume (ChPV), perivascular space volume (PVSV), the free water index (FWI), and the DTI-ALPS index, following habitual sleep (6-8 hours in bed), sleep restriction (3-6 hours in bed), and sleep deprivation (22-40 hours wakefulness). Sleep deprivation was primarily associated with decreased PVSV and ALPS and increased FWI; sleep restriction with the inverse pattern. However, coupling between MRI indices was limited, and models assuming a shared underlying glymphatic system underperformed. Age-related alterations were dissociable from sleep-related alterations and mimicked patterns previously interpreted as glymphatic dysfunction in the literature. Moreover, PVSV increased during the day, whereas ALPS and FWI followed a divergent, anticorrelated trajectory. Our findings suggest that these MRI indices reflect distinct physiological processes; and that sleep loss may influence brain fluid dynamics primarily by modulating inflow resistance through expansion and contraction of the PVS.

papers.title: Autonomic and Cortical Signatures of Sleepiness After Prolonged Sleep Deprivation: Pupillary Reflex, Hippus Oscillations, and Visual Evoked Potentials.
papers.abstract: To define physiologically interpretable visual biomarkers of progressive sleepiness during 48-hour total sleep deprivation and determine whether pupillary and cortical visual measures detect changes not captured by brief behavioral or resting cardiovascular assessments. Twenty-four healthy adults completed one rested baseline assessment and eight supervised deprivation sessions across 48 hours of continuous wakefulness. The protocol included digital pupillometry during the pupillary light reflex (PLR) and Pupillary Sleepiness Test (PST), pattern-reversal and flash visual evoked potentials (VEPs), Stanford Sleepiness Scale (SSS) ratings, selected psychophysiological tasks, and resting blood pressure and heart rate measurements. PLR latency, reaction duration, and time to minimum diameter changed early, indicating slowed reflex timing. With advanced deprivation, DDil1 and DDil2 (pupil diameters at predefined early and late stages of redilation) decreased, identifying them as recovery-phase markers beyond classical PLR indices. The absolute Pupillary Unrest Index (PUI), measuring spontaneous pupillary oscillations (hippus), rose during the first deprivation night and remained elevated; the pupil-size-normalized rPUI followed slightly later, whereas mean pupil diameter was less informative. VEPs added a cortical layer: peak latencies of the pattern-reversal P100 and N135 and flash N3 and P3 components were delayed after prolonged wakefulness. SSS ratings increased progressively, while brief psychophysiological task performance and resting cardiovascular measures remained comparatively stable. Prolonged wakefulness was reflected by a temporally organized visual biomarker profile spanning phasic pupillary reflex timing, dilation-phase recovery, tonic pupillary instability, and late cortical visual-response slowing. These findings support a candidate multimodal, non-invasive framework for objective assessment of progressive sleepiness.

papers.title: Divergence in sleep architecture associated with interspecific shifts in memory investment
papers.abstract: Sleep plays a critical role in stabilising memory. However, whether the architecture of sleep co-evolves with investment in learning and memory is unknown. To address this, we exploit the extreme levels of neural and behavioural divergence among Heliconiini butterflies. Compared to other Heliconiini, Heliconius have massively expanded mushroom bodies, the insect centres of learning and memory, which are associated with specific enhancements in visual learning and memory. Using a purpose-built video system, machine learning-facilitated behavioural tracking, and in-depth analysis of micro-behaviours during nighttime quiescence, we describe multi-state sleep in Heliconius melpomene and an outgroup Heliconiini, Dryas iulia. In both species, sleep is predominantly composed of quiet sleep, however, Heliconius and Dryas deviate in specific features. In Dryas iulia, quiet sleep is characterised by highly stereotyped, rhythmic antennal oscillations. Conversely, the antennae of Heliconius melpomene remain largely motionless but occasionally perform large movements which interrupt quiet sleep. These antennal deflections are associated with bouts of activity that include increased overall antennal displacement, isolated head twitching, proboscis movements and less frequently, wing movements. While these episodes were also seen in Dryas iulia, they were considerably less frequent. We further demonstrate that the behavioural profile of these active sleep bouts is constituently different from bouts of induced wakefulness, providing experimental support for multi-state sleep in Lepidoptera. This work shows that Heliconius melpomene, a species distinguished by its expanded mushroom bodies, exhibits more frequent bouts of active sleep than the outgroup species Dryas iulia. These findings raise the possibility that increased investment in learning and memory, as well as the structures that support it, may be associated with changes in sleep architecture.

papers.title: A Benchmark of Unsupervised Circadian Phase Inference Methods for Bulk Transcriptomic Data.
papers.abstract: Circadian phase can be inferred from gene expression when sample collection times are unavailable, but the available methods have not been systematically compared. We compared ten unsupervised phase inference methods and two clock-gene baselines on 25 datasets with reference times (16 real datasets from five studies and 9 simulations). The primary measure was the aligned circular mean absolute error (MAE), with a permutation test for significance, circular correlations and gene-level reconstruction of rhythmicity, acrophase and amplitude were secondary outcomes. CHIRAL had the lowest mean MAE (1.80 h, 95% confidence interval 1.21-2.97 h from resampling study families). The two clock-gene baselines (2.15 and 2.20 h) were next, followed by TEMPO, CYCLOPS and CYCLOPS 2.0 (2.49-2.80 h), and the confidence intervals of these six overlapped substantially. The other six methods had mean errors of 3.91-4.86 h, compared with 5.08-5.23 h for permuted phases. Accuracy depended on the dataset and on the strength of clock-gene rhythms, and, for several methods, on the random seed and the adjustment for batch or covariates. When the inferred phases were used to analyse gene rhythms in 22 datasets, the four leading methods identified rhythmic genes with a median ROC AUC of 0.64-0.70 and recovered gene acrophases with a median error of 0.18-0.64 h. In two mouse datasets without collection times, agreement with external reference acrophases differed between methods and tissues.

papers.title: Enhancing the Suppression of Unwanted Memories During NREM Sleep.
papers.abstract: Memory suppression, the ability to exclude unwanted memories from awareness, plays a critical role in maintaining mental well-being. Whereas the mechanisms of memory suppression during wakefulness have been extensively studied, the effects of sleep on this process and its associated neural mechanisms remain understudied. Targeted memory reactivation, an experimental approach for investigating the relationship between sleep and memory processing, provides a unique opportunity to further explore this relationship. Here, we combined the Think/No-Think paradigm with targeted memory reactivation to investigate whether and how reactivating suppression processes during sleep engages its associated neural mechanisms and influences later memory performance. Participants first learned cue-associate word pairs. They were then presented with trials, each exposing a cue word, preceded by an auditory instruction requiring the participant to either retrieve or suppress the corresponding target word. Subsequently, during NREM sleep, we unobtrusively re-presented the auditory tone signaling the instruction to suppress retrieval. We found that cueing people to suppress in this manner significantly enhanced suppression-induced forgetting on a later post-sleep test, compared to pairs that were not cued during sleep. Electroencephalogram analyses revealed that reactivation of suppression instructions increased theta power and reduced the coupling strength between spindles and the slow oscillation (SO) up-states. Importantly, only reduced SO up-state-spindle coupling predicted poorer later memory retrieval for suppressed pairs. The present results suggest that the disruption of neural synchrony between SO up-state and spindles during sleep plays a critical role in enhancing subsequent suppression-induced forgetting.

papers.title: Time-dependent efficacy of vitamin D3 against chronic stress-induced behavioral and circadian deficits via the hepatic VDR-clock axis.
papers.abstract: Vitamin D3 (VitD3) is an essential fat-soluble micronutrient that protects against chronic stress-related disorders through its neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects. Major depressive disorder is accompanied by circadian rhythm (CR) disruption, and evidence from chrono-nutrition studies suggests that nutrient effects are strongly influenced by administration timing. However, whether VitD3 efficacy against chronic stress depends on intervention timing remains unclear. This study assessed the chrono-nutrition potential of VitD3 in a mouse model of chronic stress. Mice subjected to 4 weeks of chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) received daily VitD3 either in the morning (AM) or evening (PM). VitD3 treatment mitigated CUMS-induced behavioral impairments, neuroinflammation, and neuronal damage in a time-dependent manner, with superior outcomes observed with PM administration. PM administration enhanced anxiety- and depression-like behaviors, hippocampal integrity, TNF-α levels, sleep duration, and serotonin synthesis. Mechanistically, PM administration more effectively restored hepatic Vdr rhythmic oscillation, coupled with re-synchronization of the core clock network. Genetic validation in Caenorhabditis elegans further supported the essential role of VDR in circadian restoration. This study is the first to reveal the time-dependent antidepressant effects of VitD3 and identify the VDR-circadian clock axis as the underlying mechanism. These findings highlight the importance of intervention timing for VitD3 efficacy and support precision nutrition strategies aligned with CR for stress disorders.

papers.title: Changes and trajectories in sleep duration and risk of premature all-cause and cardiovascular disease mortality.
papers.abstract: BackgroundWhile substantial evidence indicates an association between sleep and a range of chronic conditions, the potential impact of longitudinal changes in sleep on the risk of premature mortality remains poorly characterized.MethodsWe conducted a population-based cohort study using data from The Rural Chinese Cohort Study. Baseline assessments were performed during 2007-2008, with two subsequent follow-up surveys conducted in 2013-2014 and 2018-2020. A total of 13621 adults aged ⩾18 years were included after excluding participants with missing sleep duration data at baseline or the first follow-up or aged ⩾70 years at baseline. Cox proportional hazards regression models were employed to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the associations of relative changes and trajectories of sleep duration with premature all-cause and cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality.ResultsDuring a median follow-up of 5.07 years, the relative change in sleep duration was significantly associated with the risks of premature all-cause and CVD mortality. Compared with participants with stable sleep duration (-15% to 15%), those with a ⩾30% increase in sleep duration had a higher risk of premature all-cause (HR 1.78, 95% CI 1.28-2.47) and CVD mortality (HR 2.20, 95% CI 1.42-3.41). Sleep trajectory analyses suggested that transitions toward long sleep duration (>9 h/day) were associated with an increased risk of premature CVD mortality.ConclusionsMaintaining a stable healthy sleep duration might be important for reducing the risk of premature all-cause and CVD mortality. These findings highlight the potential value of monitoring dynamic changes in sleep duration as a modifiable target for health promotion.

papers.title: Circadian phase alignment promotes survival under predictive oxidative stress.
papers.abstract: Circadian clocks are endogenous time-keeping mechanisms that continue to oscillate with a period that approximates 24 h in the absence of cyclic environmental cues. This free-running period (FRP) varies from species to species and can vary within species across latitudinal clines. Because natural environments provide daily cues that reset circadian clocks to exactly 24 h, the importance of the FRP length is unclear. Using the cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus we show that the FRP length alters the alignment of a biological process with an environmental reference, known as phase angle of entrainment, across seasonal photoperiods, thereby repositioning stress-response programs relative to the external environment. This phase relationship affects the overall fitness of the organism: strains that position stress-response programs to peak at the time at which the stressor peaks outcompete their early- or late-peaking counterparts. Our results suggest that the FRP length is selected for its ability to adjust the phase angle of entrainment across seasonal photoperiods: the wild-type FRP length was uniquely plastic in its ability to adjust stress-response programs to coincide with the stressor in all photoperiod conditions. Circadian clocks are nearly universal biological timing systems that allow organisms to anticipate daily environmental changes, optimize environmental resources, and avoid environmental threats. We investigated which features of clock function promote survival fitness and which environmental conditions provide selection. A long-standing hypothesis is that the phase relationship between the internal timing mechanism and the external environment is critical for the circadian clock to confer a fitness advantage. However, because this phase relationship is influenced by the circadian period, tests of this hypothesis confound the two features. We experimentally decoupled the free-running period and the environmental phase relationship to show that the phase relationship, rather than the free-running period, confers fitness under environmental conditions that impose a selection.

papers.title: Altered EEG-derived co-fluctuation structure in disorders of consciousness.
papers.abstract: EEG-derived functional connectivity (FC) enables high-temporal-resolution probing of neural mechanisms underlying disorders of consciousness (DOC). Unlike stationary conventional FC, dynamic FC (dFC) captures fast transient neural coupling. Recent fMRI studies introduced a co‑fluctuation framework to track moment‑to‑moment connectivity change, yet whether such co-fluctuation features can quantify consciousness status remains elusive. Here, we adapt this established co-fluctuation paradigm to resting-state EEG to characterize the temporal architectures of EEG-derived FC across varying conscious states. We decomposed the co-fluctuation time series into high-amplitude frames (HAF) and low-amplitude frames (LAF), comparing their dynamics between real brain data and null models. We then analyzed co-fluctuation activities across consciousness levels at both global and local spatial scales, examining spatial variability in these patterns. By integrating HAF and LAF parameters, we evaluated their diagnostic potential for distinguishing DOC states. Results revealed reduced stability of co-fluctuations with loss of consciousness, accompanied by a shift toward random system dynamics. DOC patients exhibited reduced spatial and temporal heterogeneity in co-fluctuation activities compared to healthy controls. Both high- and low-amplitude patterns provided useful metrics for detecting consciousness levels. These findings offer novel insights into the dynamic organization of brain networks in DOC, emphasizing the significance of co-fluctuation dynamics in characterizing brain states and suggesting potential biomarkers for assessing consciousness levels. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11571-026-10580-7.

papers.title: Circadian Clock Coordination of the Notch-to-Wnt Signaling Switch Promotes Regenerative Myogenesis
papers.abstract: Regenerative deficits of muscle stem cells (MuSCs) contribute to progressive muscle loss in muscular dystrophy. Successful regenerative repair requires a Notch to Wnt switch to allow MuSC expansion and myogenic differentiation, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Leveraging complementary genetic and pharmacological approaches, here we identify the circadian clock as a key regulator of the Notch to Wnt signaling transition to promote regeneration with therapeutic potential for dystrophic disease. Circadian clock activity marks cycling myogenic progenitors during muscle regeneration, and clock induction occurs in concert with Notch activation. We identify that key components of the Notch pathway are direct transcriptional targets of the clock that were induced by clock activation. Mechanistically, clock coordination of Notch and Wnt signaling promoted MuSC proliferative expansion while facilitating myogenic progression during regeneration. Importantly, this clock-regulated mechanism was preserved in dystrophin-deficient mouse and human myoblasts, and clock-activating compounds enhanced regenerative myogenesis in dystrophic muscle. Collectively, our findings uncover a circadian clock-controlled mechanism that orchestrates regenerative signaling transition with potential for therapeutic targeting to restore regenerative capacity in dystrophic disease.

papers.title: The use of wearable devices in the community to detect symptom severity and relapse of psychosis: A systematic review.
papers.abstract: Psychosis is a debilitating illness, marked by frequent relapses that are difficult to manage. Community mental health care can be reactive and inconsistent, but wearable devices offer the potential to monitor clinical status using biometric data (e.g. sleep-wake cycle, physical activity, heart rate). This study evaluates the feasibility of using wearable devices and examines if they can detect early warning signs of clinical deterioration and relapse in people with psychosis in the community setting. A systematic review following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, consisting of 18- to 65-year-olds living in the community with psychosis. Only studies using a wearable device (research- or consumer-grade) with direct skin contact measuring biometric markers (e.g. actigraphy, electrodermal activity, heart rate variability) were included. Twenty-seven studies met the inclusion criteria, with 18 unique studies. Schizophrenia spectrum disorders were the predominant diagnoses, and the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale was the most used clinical outcome measure. Most studies (12/18) were short-term (<28 days). Physical activity via actigraphy (n = 18) was most commonly examined, followed by sleep-wake cycle (n = 16) and heart rate (n = 13), with some integrating smartphone-based ecological momentary assessment (n = 8). Three unique studies attempted to detect relapse by combining wearable data with clinical data. Overall, most studies carried a serious risk of bias, primarily due to confounding and selective reporting. The use of wearable devices in community settings is feasible for monitoring the severity of psychotic symptoms and may detect relapse, though findings are limited by heterogeneity in wearable and clinical measures and study design.

papers.title: Advanced Two-Stage Authentication with EEG: Inter-Subject P300 ERP Classification Using EEGNet for User Recognition.
papers.abstract: A reliable biometric system is crucial in modern security challenges. EEG signals offer a promising alternative to conventional biometrics due to their uniqueness, forgery resistance, and long-term stability. Among EEG-based approaches, P300 event-related potentials (ERPs) are widely studied for their robustness in distinguishing individuals. This study proposes a two-stage authentication framework integrating user identification (multi-class classification) and authentication (binary classification) for enhanced security. A comprehensive EEG preprocessing pipeline including bandpass filtering, epoch rejection, temporal cropping, and downsampling was implemented to improve signal quality and extract cleaner P300 responses. EEGNet, a lightweight convolutional neural network designed for EEG analysis, was used for feature extraction and classification. 16 participants across three sessions evaluated the system robustness under cross-session conditions. The framework demonstrated strong generalization, achieving up to 95% precision and a mean accuracy of 96.10% for both identification and authentication. These results highlight the potential of EEGNet user authentication using P300 ERPs, offering insights into optimal preprocessing and deep learning methods for EEG-based security. This study underscores brainwave-driven authentication as a secure and viable alternative to traditional biometrics, paving the way for real-time applications in cybersecurity and identity verification.

papers.title: Clocks In Sync: A mixed methods pilot feasibility trial of blue-light blocking therapy and time-restricted eating, alone or in combination for mania in bipolar disorder.
papers.abstract: Sleep and circadian disruptions are common in bipolar disorder (BD). Persons with lived and living experience (PWLEs) find chronotherapies to be of great interest, especially blue-blocking glasses (BBG, targeting the central biological clock) and time-restricted eating (TRE, targeting peripheral clocks). We conducted a mixed methods randomized, three group parallel pilot trial (clinicaltrials.gov: NCT06504342) to assess the feasibility of BBG and/or TRE (10: 14 of diurnal eating to nocturnal fasting informed by PWLE input) as an adjunctive treatment for inpatients with DSM-5-defined mania and a Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS) ≥ 20. Participants were randomized 1:1:1 to TRE (BBG-/TRE+), BBG (BBG+/TRE-) or both (BBG+/TRE+). Feasibility was assessed through monitoring of adherence and qualitative semi-structured interviews with participants and staff were conducted to identify any challenges/barriers to implementation, and what supports might be needed. Change in the YMRS from blinded raters was a secondary outcome. Twenty-one eligible participants consented for the trial and 80% of participants (16/20) were mostly adherent or better with no differences in adherence across groups. Qualitative data highlights patient interest in chronotherapy interventions and staff support of integrating them in practice. There was also interest in shorter or flexible timing of the studied chronotherapies. Greater improvements were observed in the BBG+ groups compared to BBG-/TRE+ on the YMRS. Most inpatients with BD can adhere to circadian interventions requiring active participation in high acuity, inpatient settings. Our pilot study may inform future studies or clinical implementation of these and other low cost and scalable chronotherapies.

papers.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Sleep Disturbances: A Narrative Review of Bidirectional Mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic autoimmune disease in which sleep disturbances are common and closely linked to pain, fatigue, mood symptoms, physical dysfunction, and disease activity. This narrative review synthesizes clinical and mechanistic evidence for a bidirectional relationship between RA and impaired sleep while distinguishing diagnosed sleep disorders from transdiagnostic sleep symptoms. RA-related inflammation, pain, stiffness, and psychological comorbidity may impair sleep through peripheral-to-central inflammatory signaling, altered monoamine metabolism, circadian disruption, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysfunction, autonomic hyperarousal, and central sensitization. Conversely, insufficient or fragmented sleep may disrupt immune and circadian homeostasis, amplify pro-inflammatory signaling and pain sensitivity, and thereby worsen RA symptoms and possibly disease activity. However, much of the available evidence is cross-sectional, based on patient-reported sleep, or derived from small treatment studies, so direct causality and the independent contribution of individual pathways remain uncertain. Evidence from cytokine-blocking and sleep-directed interventions suggests potential benefit, but improvements may be mediated through changes in pain, fatigue, mood, and inflammatory activity. Age, sex, adiposity, medications, depression, anxiety, and sleep-disorder phenotype further modify these associations. Clinically, RA care should distinguish insomnia, obstructive sleep apnea, restless legs syndrome, circadian problems, and non-diagnostic sleep symptoms, then combine optimized RA and pain management with disorder-specific sleep treatment. Longitudinal multimodal cohorts and adequately powered trials using both patient-reported and objective sleep outcomes are priorities.

papers.title: Feasibility of Vibrotactile P50 Sensory-Gating Assessment Using Portable EEG
papers.abstract: Sensory gating (SG), most commonly quantified using the auditory P50 event-related potential elicited by a paired "double-click" paradigm, is a well-established biomarker of early sensory inhibition that reflects the brain's ability to suppress responses to repetitive sensory input. Although auditory SG paradigms have been widely used in both research and clinical settings, they impose an unavoidable auditory load and are generally limited to controlled laboratory environments, reducing their suitability for ecological monitoring and applications in which auditory resources must remain available. This study evaluated the feasibility of a portable vibrotactile sensory-gating system designed to assess inhibitory processing without engaging the auditory or visual modalities. Fifteen healthy adult participants completed both auditory and vibrotactile paired-stimulus conditions using a within-subject experimental design. Vibrotactile stimuli were delivered through transducers positioned on the volar surface of the forearm while electroencephalographic (EEG) activity was recorded using a 32-channel Emotiv EPOC Flex system. Event-related responses were extracted and analyzed using conventional sensory-gating metrics to enable direct comparison between modalities. Vibrotactile stimulation elicited time-locked P50 responses with attenuation of S2 relative to S1. Mean S2/S1 ratios were 0.521 +- 0.041 for the auditory condition and 0.524 +- 0.064 for the vibrotactile condition. The paired difference was 0.0029 (95% CI, -0.0221 to 0.0279), t(14) = 0.249, p = 0.807, dz = 0.064. No statistically significant difference was detected between modalities in this sample. These group-level findings support further evaluation of portable vibrotactile P50 measurement.

papers.title: Clinical features of the postictal state in adults with epilepsy: A cross-sectional survey.
papers.abstract: Persons with epilepsy may experience many postictal symptoms after a seizure, which can significantly impact quality of life. We aimed to determine the frequency, duration, and severity of postictal symptoms to better characterize the postictal period. Our cross-sectional questionnaire was adapted from a prior pediatric postictal survey. Face and content validity were evaluated by epilepsy experts and patients from the Calgary Epilepsy Program (CEP). The survey was pilot tested and modified, consisting of 14 physical, cognitive, and psychiatric postictal signs and symptoms. Consecutive CEP adults who had agreed to participate in research and experienced a seizure in the prior 2 years were approached. CEP clinical data were used to supplement survey data. Frequency of factors alleviating and exacerbating postictal symptoms were examined. Spearman's rho was used to explore associations between survey and CEP registry data with statistical significance at ≤ 0.05. Of 351 patients approached, 313 agreed to participate (89%). Fourteen were lost after consent was obtained, and 15 were excluded (incomplete surveys, missing registry data, not having epilepsy). Of the 298 final participants, 54% were female, mean age was 40 years (SD = 15.6), and 95% (282/298) experienced at least one postictal symptom. The three most frequent postictal symptoms were fatigue, sleepiness, or tiredness (84%), confusion or difficulty thinking clearly (75%), and memory problems (69%). For eight of 14 captured postictal symptoms, the most frequently reported symptom duration was <5 min. Mean postictal symptom burden score was correlated with patient reported quality of life and epilepsy-related disability measures. Sleep or rest, medication, and food or drinks were the most common alleviating factors. Lack of rest or sleep, and stress most often exacerbated postictal symptoms. This work contributes toward a better understanding of the postictal period and informs the development of future interventions to minimize the impact of the postictal period in epilepsy.

papers.title: Lifestyle-Based Interventions for Major Depressive Disorder and Their Role Alongside Antidepressant Treatment: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) remains disabling despite effective pharmacotherapy, and many patients experience an incomplete response or residual symptoms. This systematic review evaluated randomized trials of structured exercise or mind-body exercise, sleep/circadian and bright-light interventions, whole-diet interventions, and multicomponent lifestyle programs delivered alongside antidepressant treatment in adults with current MDD. PubMed, Europe PMC, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception through September 15, 2026, with supplementary citation searching of eligible reports and relevant reviews. The electronic searches identified 1,310 records. After the removal of 333 duplicate bibliographic records and one non-usable record, 976 records underwent screening. Thirty-eight reports were assessed at full text. Following eligibility assessment and final verification, 26 eligible reports remained from the original search, and eight additional eligible reports were identified through supplementary citation searching. The final review included 34 reports representing 29 independent randomized studies. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool, certainty of evidence was evaluated using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE), and results were synthesized without meta-analysis because substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity made a pooled estimate inappropriate. Structured exercise showed the most consistent favorable signal, although effects were generally smaller or less certain in trials using active comparators. Sleep/circadian and bright-light interventions showed possible short-term benefits in selected studies, but findings varied by intervention, comparator, and assessment time, and sustained benefits were inconsistent. Evidence for multicomponent lifestyle programs was sparse, and no eligible randomized trial evaluated a whole-diet intervention alone as an adjunct to antidepressant treatment. Overall certainty of the evidence was low to very low because of risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. Lifestyle-based interventions may provide additional benefit as adjuncts to antidepressant treatment, particularly structured exercise and selected sleep/circadian interventions; however, the magnitude and durability of benefit remain uncertain. Substitution of lifestyle interventions for antidepressant medication was not evaluated in this review.

papers.title: Accelerometry-Derived REM Sleep Behavior Disorder Score Is Associated with Incident Parkinson's Disease in the UK Biobank
papers.abstract: Estimating Parkinson's disease (PD) risk years before diagnosis remains an unmet need. We applied a validated machine learning classifier for REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) detection to 7-day wrist accelerometry data in 87,975 UK Biobank participants followed for 10 years. Participants in the highest RBD risk stratum (>99th percentile) had an approximately fivefold increased hazard of incident PD compared with the lowest-risk group (0-90th percentile), with a dose-dependent relationship across the full score distribution. Among non-converters, higher RBD-classifier scores were associated with baseline cognitive deficits and greater burden of autonomic and psychiatric prodromal features. The association with incident PD remained independent of PD polygenic risk score, while RBD-classifier score and genetic risk were synergistic. The combined high-risk group achieved a positive likelihood ratio of 7.91, approximately threefold higher than questionnaire-based RBD screening. At this High-risk threshold over the 10-year horizon, the classifier showed a sensitivity of 7.4%, specificity of 99.2%, positive predictive value of 7.5%, and negative predictive value of 99.2% for incident PD (N=50,816). These findings support wrist accelerometry as a scalable, high-specificity approach for prodromal PD risk enrichment.

papers.title: Real-time wearable detection of respiratory infections in pediatric transplant households.
papers.abstract: Consumer-grade wearables can continuously and longitudinally measure health signals such as heart rate (HR), activity, and sleep. While changes in these signals have been implicated in the early detection of infection (e.g., influenza, SARS-CoV-2) and real-time alerting systems have been developed, evidence from prospective deployment in pediatric transplant households remains limited. Here, we study the application of a resting heart rate (RHR)-based real-time alerting algorithm to detect respiratory virus infection in a cohort of solid organ transplant recipients and their household members (n=146) in a Phase IV clinical trial ( NCT06161454 ). Reliable and efficient alerting for infection events may be particularly relevant for this population, enabling isolation, clinical management, and/or treatment. Of 31 antigen-test outcomes, nearly all (29/31, 93.5%) correspond to either influenza, COVID, or other patient-reported symptoms. We describe RHR, HR, activity, and sleep/circadian rhythm features around clinical alarm events, identifying candidate features for further investigation and algorithm improvement.

papers.title: Evidence of high rates of burnout symptoms in a cohort with cluster headache.
papers.abstract: Cluster headache is a debilitating primary headache disorder. During active bouts, headache attacks occur daily and can last up to 3 h. Besides the excruciating pain, the disorder can greatly impact a patient's mental health, sleep, and life quality. The reoccurring attacks as well as sleep problems may lead to energy depletion and burnout symptoms, which can limit a person's ability to participate in society to the extent they would like to. Our aim was to investigate the extent of burnout symptoms in a Swedish cluster headache cohort using a cross-sectional approach. We further wanted to study if burnout symptoms can be linked to disease status-and if sex, lifestyle factors, or any specific clinical characteristics may be linked to change in burnout symptoms. Between January 2024 and September 2025, the Shirom-Melamed Burnout Questionnaire was sent out via the Research Electronic Data Capture platform to 839 study participants with cluster headache. Global scores from the questionnaire were compared between study participants in active bout and remission. Likewise, the scores were analyzed between participants whose remission period had lasted longer than 5 years (long-term) compared to less than 5 years (short-term). Lifestyle and clinical factors were further analyzed in study participants with high Shirom-Melamed Burnout Questionnaire scores (global score >3.75). The total number of individuals included in the analysis was 373/839 (44.5%). Scores above threshold (>3.75) were recorded in 65.9% (58/88) of study participants in an active bout compared to 37.5% (90/240) in the remission group (odds ratio [OR] = 3.22, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.93-5.38; p < 0.001). Participants in short-term remission similarly had a higher percentage of scores above threshold compared to participants in long-term remission (42.0% [73/174] vs. 22.2% [12/54], OR = 2.53, 95% CI = 1.25-5.14; p = 0.009). Participants with burnout scores above 3.75 were more likely to be females (OR = 3.25, 95% CI = 2.04-5.19; pcorrected <0.001) and report sleep deprivation as an attack trigger (OR = 2.24, 95% CI = 1.32-3.82; pcorrected = 0.034). Participants with cluster headache in our Swedish cohort reported higher scores for burnout symptoms, particularly during active bout. For participants in remission, the burnout symptoms score was inversely correlated to the number of years since their last active headache bout. When managing cluster headache in a clinical setting, it should be taken into consideration that this patient group has a substantial risk for developing burnout symptoms both in and out of an active bout. Future studies should evaluate how to best support patients with cluster headache handling exhaustion and promote recovery to improve their quality of life.

papers.title: Comparison of quality of life between docetaxel and weekly paclitaxel in the neoadjuvant or adjuvant treatment of breast cancer.
papers.abstract: Taxane-based chemotherapy remains a cornerstone of neoadjuvant and adjuvant treatment for stage II-III breast cancer. Weekly paclitaxel and 3-weekly docetaxel exhibit comparable oncologic efficacy but differ in toxicity profiles and treatment schedules. This study aimed to compare longitudinal patient-reported quality-of-life (QoL) outcomes between these two taxane regimens. This single-center observational cohort study included 82 patients with stage II-III breast cancer who received anthracycline-based chemotherapy followed by either docetaxel every 3 weeks (n=55) or weekly paclitaxel (n=27). QoL was assessed at four time points using the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Breast (FACT-B), Beck Anxiety Inventory, Beck Depression Inventory, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, and Quality of Life Enjoyment and Satisfaction Questionnaire. Longitudinal changes and between-group differences were also analyzed. Baseline QoL scores were comparable between groups. During active treatment, both regimens were associated with deterioration in several QoL domains, with recovery observed following treatment completion. At the third assessment time point, corresponding to peak treatment burden, patients receiving docetaxel reported significantly higher depressive symptoms and lower life satisfaction compared with those receiving weekly paclitaxel. However, global FACT-B scores or sleep quality showed no significant differences at any time point. Hematologic adverse events, particularly anemia and neutropenia, were more frequent in the docetaxel group, whereas peripheral sensory neuropathy was more common with weekly paclitaxel. No grade 4 adverse events or treatment-related deaths occurred. Weekly paclitaxel and 3-weekly docetaxel yielded broadly comparable longitudinal QoL outcomes in curative-intent breast cancer treatment. Docetaxel was associated with a greater short-term psychological burden during peak chemotherapy exposure. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating patient-reported outcomes into treatment selection and supportive care strategies.

papers.title: Heterogeneous perceived stress profiles and static-dynamic symptom networks of PTSD, anxiety, depression, and insomnia in firefighters: An integrated latent profile and network analysis.
papers.abstract: Firefighters are routinely exposed to occupational stress and potentially traumatic events, yet heterogeneity in perceived stress and its associations with psychopathological symptom patterns remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to identify perceived stress profiles in Chinese firefighters and examine profile-specific cross-sectional and longitudinal associations among psychopathological symptoms. A total of 8428 Chinese firefighters were recruited, and two assessments were conducted nine months apart. Latent profile analysis was used to identify perceived stress profiles. Regularized partial correlation networks and cross-lagged panel networks were then estimated within each profile to examine cross-sectional and prospective associations among post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety, depression, and insomnia symptoms. Three perceived stress profiles were identified: Task-related thinking (55.59%), Consistent stress perception (23.92%), and Imbalanced stress perception (20.49%). The Imbalanced stress perception profile reported the highest levels of perceived stress, whereas the Consistent stress perception profile exhibited the greatest psychopathological burden. Cross-sectional networks revealed distinct profile-specific symptom connectivity patterns, with sleep disturbance, arousal, and feelings of failure showing the highest expected influence, respectively. Longitudinal networks further revealed profile-specific temporal associations, with arousal, intrusion, and negative cognition/mood showing the highest out-expected influence, respectively. Low sleep satisfaction consistently showed the highest in-expected influence across profiles. Perceived stress configurations may provide complementary insights into psychopathological symptom burden beyond overall stress severity among firefighters. The profile-specific cross-sectional and longitudinal symptom associations highlight the potential value of person-centered approaches for mental health assessment and risk stratification, while their implications for targeted interventions require further prospective and interventional validation.

papers.title: Longitudinal Pain Profiles and Their Clinical and Genetic Correlates in 624,996 U.S. Veterans.
papers.abstract: Pain varies in its intensity and course, yet much of our understanding of pain is based on cross-sectional assessments or longitudinal studies of selected clinical populations. Routinely collected electronic health record data may enable characterization of longitudinal pain patterns at scale. To identify longitudinal pain profiles among U.S. Veterans and characterize their clinical and polygenic correlates. Cohort study using electronic health record and genomic data from the Million Veteran Program, with up to 16 years of pain assessments collected between 2000 to 2025. U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs health care system. Million Veteran Program participants assigned to African-like, Admixed American-like, East Asian-like, European-like, or South Asian-like genetically inferred ancestry groups who have at least three years of outpatient numeric rating scale pain records. Outpatient pain ratings and polygenic scores for psychiatric, sleep, and substance use traits. Pain profiles were identified using Gaussian finite mixture modeling of pain intensity, directional change, and within-person variability. Profiles were characterized by pain, psychiatric and substance use diagnoses, opioid exposure, body mass index, and polygenic scores. Among 624,996 participants (Mean [SD] age at first pain rating=53.4 [13.5] years; 568,833 [91.0%] male), 51,731,567 outpatient pain ratings were analyzed. Three profiles were identified: stable no pain, stable mild pain, and mild-to-moderate increasing pain. Compared with the stable no pain profile, the increasing pain profile had higher odds of chronic pain (OR=21.14 [95% CI: 18.96-23.57]), opioid use disorder (OR=9.32 [95% CI: 8.31-10.45]), opioid exposure (OR=8.61 [95% CI: 8.41-8.83]), major depressive disorder (OR=3.77 [95% CI: 3.67-3.87]), and posttraumatic stress disorder (OR=3.72 [95% CI: 3.61-3.84]). Associations were attenuated but remained after adjustment for mean pain severity. Polygenic scores for depression, insomnia, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and tobacco use disorder were the most consistent predictors of increasing pain across the three largest genetically inferred ancestry groups. Longitudinal modeling of routinely collected pain scores identified pain profiles associated with clinical burden and polygenic liability. These profiles captured clinically meaningful information beyond mean pain severity alone, highlighting the value of longitudinal pain phenotyping in electronic health record data. Question: Can pain scores collected in outpatient care identify clinically meaningful pain profiles among U.S. Veterans?Findings: In this cohort study of 624,996 Veterans with more than 51 million pain ratings across up to 16 years, three pain profiles were identified: stable no pain, stable mild pain, and mild-tomoderate increasing pain. Profiles differed in clinical burden even after accounting for mean pain severity and were associated with polygenic liability for psychiatric, sleep, and substance use traits.Meaning: Routinely collected pain scores can be used to characterize heterogeneity in the course of pain and factors associated with more burdensome pain patterns.

papers.title: Risk of obstructive sleep apnea in patients with polycystic ovary syndrome by body mass index: Retrospective cohort study with Korean nationwide population-based cohort.
papers.abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a gynecologic endocrine disorder affecting various aspects of women's health. Research examining the association between PCOS, obesity, and obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in Korean populations remains limited. We assessed OSA risk in Korean with PCOS, considering body mass index (BMI). We conducted a retrospective cohort study using health insurance claims data from the National Health Insurance Service. We selected 33 638 people with PCOS and 98 110 controls with available BMI data. This is a subgroup representing our previous retrospective cohort study, which identified the relationship between PCOS and several mental disorders. Hazard ratios (HR) for PCOS were calculated using Cox proportional hazards regression models. Obese individuals had a higher prevalence of OSA (0.60% in people with PCOS, 0.20% in controls) compared with the non-obese individuals (0.12% in people with PCOS, 0.13% in controls). PCOS (hazard ratio [HR]: 1.483, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.029-2.137) and BMI (HR: 1.104, 95% CI: 1.069-1.141) were associated with an increased risk of OSA. Our findings suggest that the risk of OSA is higher in people with PCOS. This research holds significance by indicating that obesity at the time of PCOS diagnosis could serve as a potential predictor for OSA. This study supports international PCOS guidelines that recommend screening and managing OSA.

papers.title: The Relationship of Triglyceride/Glucose Index with Disease Severity, Sleep, and Cognitive Functions in Patients with Geriatric Depression: A Comparative Cross-Sectional Study with Healthy Controls.
papers.abstract: This cross-sectional study investigated the association between the TyG index - a peripheral insulin resistance marker - and depression status, clinical severity, sleep quality, and cognitive functions in drug-naïve older adults compared to healthy controls. Older adults aged 60-74 (mean: 66.2 ± 3.8, range: 60-74; 65.5% depressed) comprising 76 patients with MDD and 40 controls were evaluated using GDS-15, ISI, and SMMSE. Assessor-blinded to the clinical psychiatric status of the participants. The TyG index was significantly higher in patients than controls. Within the depressed cohort (n = 76), the TyG index correlated significantly with depression severity (r = 0.401, p < .001), but its cross-sectional associations with cognitive function (p = .110) and insomnia severity (p = .163) were non-significant. In multivariate logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, education, BMI, and comorbidities, the TyG index remained independently associated with higher odds of depression status (Exp(B)=24.935, p < .001). Exploratory ROC analysis revealed that a tentative cutoff of >8.78 discriminated depressed individuals with 63.16% sensitivity and 95.00% specificity (AUC = 0.804, p < .001). The TyG index is cross-sectionallyassociated with depression status and clinical severity in drug-naïveolder adults, independent of BMI. The TyG index represents a cost-effective, noninvasive exploratory metabolic biomarker that may complement clinical screenings in late-life psychiatry.

papers.title: Perioperative non-invasive brain stimulation for the prevention of postoperative delirium: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
papers.abstract: BackgroundPostoperative delirium is a common perioperative complication. Early randomised trials suggested that non-invasive brain stimulation may reduce postoperative delirium, whereas the recent MODEST trial found no preventive benefit. We synthesised the randomised evidence for perioperative non-invasive brain stimulation. MethodsWe searched eight bibliographic databases and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to 30 September 2026 for randomised controlled trials of perioperative non-invasive brain stimulation in adults undergoing surgery. The primary outcome was postoperative delirium. Random-effects meta-analyses estimated risk ratios (RRs), mean differences, or standardised mean differences. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 and certainty of evidence using GRADE. ResultsNine trials contributed data from 1451 participants. Postoperative delirium occurred in 72 of 750 participants receiving active stimulation and 166 of 701 controls (RR 0.41, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.31-0.56; I2=24.7%; moderate-certainty evidence). Estimates also favoured stimulation for hypoactive and hyperactive delirium, but not clearly for mixed delirium. Pain, anxiety, and sleep outcomes favoured stimulation but were highly heterogeneous and supported by very-low-certainty evidence. Length of hospital stay was not reduced. Adverse events could not be pooled because reporting was incomplete and inconsistent. ConclusionsPerioperative non-invasive brain stimulation may reduce postoperative delirium, but the evidence does not establish a class effect or support routine clinical use. Geographical concentration, methodological concerns, heterogeneous stimulation protocols, and discordance with the MODEST trial warrant independent multicentre sham-controlled trials. papers.title: Differential expression of circadian clock genes and proteins in gingival tissues from patients with stage III grade B periodontitis: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: This study tested the hypothesis that gingival circadian clock gene and protein expressions differ among periodontal health, gingivitis, and stage III grade B periodontitis. Sixty systemically healthy, non-smoking individuals with regular sleep schedules, assessed by the Munich Chronotype Questionnaire, were classified as periodontally healthy (n = 20), gingivitis (n = 20), or stage III grade B periodontitis (n = 20). Gingival biopsies were obtained at a single time point (09:00 to 11:00). Clock gene and protein expressions were analyzed using RT-qPCR and Western blotting. Inflammatory mediators were quantified by RT-qPCR, and IL-1β and IL-6 protein levels were measured by ELISA. Age, sex distribution, sleep duration, and chronotype scores were comparable among groups (p > 0.05). In periodontitis, CLOCK and Per3 were higher, and CRY1, CRY2, and Rev-Erb-β were lower at both gene and protein levels (p < 0.05). Per1 and Per2 were lower at the gene level, whereas Per1 protein did not differ and Per2 protein was lower in both diseased groups (p < 0.05). BMAL1 did not differ at either level, and ROR-α gene expression did not differ (p > 0.05). In pooled exploratory analyses, proinflammatory mediators correlated positively with CLOCK and Per3 and negatively with CRY1, CRY2, Per1, Per2, and Rev-Erb-β, which in turn correlated positively with OPG (FDR-adjusted p < 0.05). RANKL was higher and OPG lower in periodontitis (p < 0.05). Clock gene expressions were also correlated with clinical periodontal parameters. Gingival tissues affected by stage III grade B periodontitis showed differential clock gene and protein expression. Because measurements were obtained at a single time point, these findings indicate differential expression rather than disrupted circadian clock function.

papers.title: Women with the FMR1 premutation: a within-family observational sibling study.
papers.abstract: Understanding the relative risk of the fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1 (FMR1) premutation (PM) versus the risk of the PM and parenting a child with fragile X syndrome (FXS) is critical for PM carriers, their families and clinicians. For this study, we compared women with the PM with their biological sisters; some sisters also had the PM and some had normal-range cytosine-guanine-guanine (CGG) repeats. The sisters were further differentiated by whether they had a child with FXS. This study of 67 women from 30 families used multilevel modelling to probe the effects of the PM with or without parenting a child with FXS, with strong control for family-of-origin factors and background genetics. Controlling for the false discovery rate, we found that mothers with the PM who had children with FXS were similar to their sisters who had the PM but did not have a child with FXS in health, sleep, social relationships, depressive symptoms and executive functioning, differing only in anxiety and stress. However, there were many differences when mothers with the PM who had children with FXS were compared with their sisters with normal-range CGGs, including greater fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome-type, depressive and anxiety symptoms, poorer sleep, greater negative support and greater stress. In this study, the effect of the PM was stronger than the effect of parenting a child with FXS. Thus, the PM phenotype should not be primarily attributed to the effect of parenting a child with FXS. Additionally, by comparing mothers who had the PM and children with FXS with their sisters without the PM, the findings confirmed the effect of this dual vulnerability and here the vulnerability emerged even with strong familial controls.

papers.title: Orforglipron for Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Results From 2 Randomized Clinical Trials (ATTAIN-OSA).
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common disorder characterized by repeated upper airway collapse during sleep that is associated with reduced quality of life and increased incidence of cardiometabolic disease. To assess the effects of orforglipron on moderate to severe OSA in adults with obesity or overweight, compared with placebo. Two 52-week, phase 3, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized clinical trials were conducted at 66 sites in the US, Argentina, Brazil, China, Czech Republic, Germany, Japan, Mexico, and Taiwan. Adults with moderate to severe OSA and body mass index (BMI; calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) of 27 or higher were enrolled between November 11, 2024, and July 23, 2025. Final follow-up occurred on July 30, 2026. Trial 1 included patients not receiving positive airway pressure treatment and trial 2 included patients receiving positive airway pressure treatment. Patients were randomized (1:1) to receive either once-daily orforglipron (maximum tolerated dose: equivalent to 9-, 14.5-, or 17.2-mg tablet dose) or placebo. The primary end point was change in apnea-hypopnea index (AHI, events/h) from baseline to week 52. Seven key multiplicity-controlled secondary end points included change in sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden, the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System Short Form Sleep-Related Impairment T-score, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein. A total of 363 patients were randomized in trial 1 (mean age, 48.4 years; BMI, 37.4; AHI, 50.7 events/h; 31.4% female) and 349 patients were randomized in trial 2 (mean age, 51.1 years; BMI, 38.6; AHI, 57.6 events/h; 26.9% female). For the treatment regimen estimand, in trial 1, the mean AHI change was -17.8 for orforglipron compared with -4.5 for placebo (difference, -13.2 [95% CI, -17.7 to -8.7]; P < .001) at 52 weeks. In trial 2, the mean AHI change was -17.3 for orforglipron and -5.3 for placebo (difference, -12.0 [95% CI, -17.1 to -6.9]; P < .001) at 52 weeks. Of 7 key secondary end points, 6 were statistically significant, favoring orforglipron. Gastrointestinal events were the most commonly reported adverse events, occurring in 123 (68.0%) participants randomized to receive orforglipron vs 68 (37.4%) randomized to receive placebo in trial 1 and in 125 (70.6%) participants randomized to receive orforglipron vs 63 (36.6%) randomized to receive placebo in trial 2. These results provide evidence for the potential use of oral orforglipron to improve sleep-disordered breathing in adults with moderate to severe OSA and obesity or overweight. papers.title: Cognitive disengagement syndrome and alexisomia: examining the moderating role of anxiety-depression symptoms, stress, and insomnia symptoms among a sample of Lebanese adults.
papers.abstract: The interplay between body and mind is at the heart of processing bodily states. Alexisomia refers to the lack of somatic awareness, whereas cognitive disengagement syndrome (CDS) is a cluster of symptoms that reflect mental sluggishness, daydreaming, and hypoactivity. Given that interoceptive accuracy relies on attention to internal signals, the hypoactive characteristics of CDS may attenuate interoceptive processing; therefore, individuals with higher CDS traits might show diminished awareness of bodily states. This study investigates the association between CDS and alexisomia, as well as the moderating effect of anxiety-depression symptoms, stress, and insomnia symptoms. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 877 Lebanese adults aged 18-70 years, recruited through snowball sampling. Data were collected using a Google Forms questionnaire that included the Adult Concentration Inventory, the Shitsu Taikan Sho Scale, the Stress Numerical Rating Scale, the Patient Health Questionnaire-4, and the Insomnia Severity Index. Of the participants, 64.3% were female, and 35.7% were male. The interaction models were adjusted over the following variables: marital status, education, and living situation. The CDS × anxiety-depression (B = -0.04, p = .011) and CDS × insomnia (B = -0.03, p = .002) interactions were significantly associated with alexisomia, whereas the CDS × stress interaction (B = -0.03, p = .076) was not statistically significant after applying heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors. At low (-1 SD), mean, and high (+1 SD) levels of anxiety - depression and insomnia, higher CDS levels were significantly associated with higher levels of alexisomia. Additionally, higher levels of anxiety-depression and insomnia symptoms attenuated the positive association between CDS traits and alexisomia. Findings highlight an interplay between symptoms of cognitive disengagement and reduced somatic awareness, while emphasizing the importance of accounting for psychological distress and sleep disturbance when studying this relationship. Understanding these interactions provides a foundation for future longitudinal research to further clarify the nature and temporal relationships among these constructs.

papers.title: Health Information Literacy Moderates the Associations of Perceived Social Support with Insomnia and Infertility Psychological Distress in Women Undergoing Assisted Reproductive Technology: A Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Psychological distress is common among women undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART). Perceived social support, insomnia, and health information literacy may be interrelated with psychological distress during fertility treatment, but their conditional relationships remain insufficiently understood. This study examined the indirect association between perceived social support and infertility psychological distress through insomnia and whether health information literacy moderated the associations among perceived social support, insomnia, and IPD. A cross-sectional survey was conducted from March to August 2024, enrolling 1007 women undergoing ART at two tertiary hospitals in Wuhan, China. Standardized instruments, including the Perceived Social Support Scale (PSS), the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), the Everyday Health Information Literacy (HIL) questionnaire, and the Infertility Psychological Distress (IPD) Scale, were utilized for data collection. Mediation and moderated mediation analyses were conducted using PROCESS Models 4 and 59 with 5000 bootstrap samples. Seven prespecified sociodemographic and clinical covariates were included in the analyses. PSS was negatively associated with IPD (B = -0.364, p < 0.001) and ISI (B = -0.094, p < 0.001). A significant indirect association between PSS and IPD through ISI was observed (indirect effect = -0.132, 95% bootstrap CI [-0.175, -0.094]). HIL significantly moderated the associations between PSS and ISI (B = -0.008, p < 0.001), between PSS and IPD (B = -0.029, p < 0.001), and between ISI and IPD (B = -0.071, p = 0.003). At higher levels of HIL, the negative associations of PSS with ISI and IPD were stronger, whereas the positive association between ISI and IPD was weaker. In this cross-sectional study, PSS was indirectly associated with IPD through ISI, and HIL modified the associations among PSS, ISI, and IPD. These findings suggest that social support, sleep problems, and HIL may be usefully considered together in psychosocial assessment during ART. Longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to determine the temporal and causal relationships among these factors.

papers.title: Avermectin poisoning with panic-like symptoms: a case series.
papers.abstract: High doses of avermectin, a macrolide derived from Streptomyces avermitilis, can cause coma, delirium, respiratory failure, hypotension, and acidosis. However, certain adverse toxicological effects and psychological implications remain unrecognized in patients undergoing parasuicide. Case 1: A 54-year-old man ingested approximately 500 mL avermectin benzylate. He was found to be somnolent 45 min later. Subsequently, the patient became unconscious with respiratory failure, hypotension, and acidosis (lactate, 16.2 mmol/L). Gastric lavage, mechanical ventilation, hemoperfusion, hemofiltration, and symptomatic treatments were administered. Three days after ingestion, the patient's primary symptoms were delirium and myoclonus, with a blood avermectin level of 110.06 μg/L. Thereafter, intermittent shaking, limb flexion, and muscle rigidity persisted. Thirteen days after ingestion, brain magnetic resonance imaging was unremarkable. Electroencephalography revealed no epileptiform discharges. After psychiatric evaluation, the patient was assessed as having panic-like symptoms, and his symptoms improved significantly with specialized treatment. Case 2: A 33-year-old man was injected with approximately 5 mL of 1% avermectin in his left forearm. Two days later, he reported significant pain and swelling along with intermittent palpitations, dizziness, and limb tremors consistent with panic-like symptoms. His blood avermectin level was 0.02 μg/mL. After 7 days of treatment, the swelling subsided, and the panic-like symptoms resolved. Avermectin poisoning causes significant toxic effects, including respiratory failure, hypotension, acidosis, coma, and delirium. Intramuscular injections may result in localized swelling. Parasuicide patients may also present with panic-like symptoms requiring careful differential diagnosis.

papers.title: A Local Enrichment Computational Framework to Identify Disease-Enriched Physical Activity Patterns
papers.abstract: Wearable accelerometers enable continuous monitoring of physical activity (PA), yet conventional summary measures and population-wide clustering approaches may overlook disease-associated behavioral heterogeneity. Here we introduce LocPA, a computational framework that identifies disease-enriched PA patterns through confounder-adjusted activity profiling, similarity network construction, local disease-enrichment testing and community detection. Applying LocPA to 24-hour accelerometry profiles from the UK Biobank, we identified two recurring PA phenotypes across six diseases spanning cardiometabolic, neurological, psychiatric, renal and cardiovascular conditions: a low-activity phenotype characterized by reduced daytime activity and a sleep-disrupted phenotype characterized by reduced daytime and elevated nocturnal activity. In hypertension and diabetes, the sleep-disrupted phenotype was associated with greater disease burden and less favorable clinical and metabolic profiles, differences not consistently captured by conventional PA summary measures. LocPA also identified disease-specific temporal patterns, particularly in Parkinsons disease. Analyses in an independent National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey cohort supported the recurrence of hypertension- and diabetes-enriched patterns across populations and accelerometry measurements. LocPA provides a flexible, disease-driven approach for uncovering clinically relevant temporal PA patterns, with potential applications in disease risk characterization and personalized behavioral interventions.

papers.title: Transient HBV entry into cerebrospinal fluid following blood-brain barrier disruption: a case of HSV-2 encephalitis with polymicrobial detection elucidated by serial targeted next-generation sequencing.
papers.abstract: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is traditionally considered a strictly hepatotropic virus, and its neuroinvasive potential remains controversial. When targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) simultaneously detects multiple viruses in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), distinguishing the true pathogen from bystander viruses poses a clinical challenge. We report a rare case of herpes simplex virus 2 (HSV-2) encephalitis with concurrent detection of HBV and human gammaherpesvirus 4 (HHV-4) in the CSF, and explore the mechanism of HBV entry into the central nervous system (CNS) through serial tNGS before and after treatment, combined with routine CSF analysis. A 42-year-old male with untreated hepatitis B presented with acute fever, frontal and temporal headache for 10 days, unresponsive to empirical anti-infective therapy. EEG revealed increased theta activity in bilateral frontal regions after hyperventilation, suggesting encephalitis. Initial CSF analysis (Day 1) showed marked pleocytosis (white blood cells 1849 × 106/L) and hemorrhagic appearance (red blood cells 1000 × 106/L), indicating acute blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption. CSF tNGS detected sequences for HSV-2, HHV-4 and HBV. High level of serum HBV DNA with positive HBsAg confirmed active HBV replication. The patient was treated with acyclovir and tenofovir alafenamide (TAF). Repeat lumbar puncture (LP) on Day 17 demonstrated normalized CSF parameters (red blood cells 0 × 106/L, white blood cells 143 × 106/L) and no viral sequences on tNGS. Serum HBV DNA decreased by approximately 2 log10 on the same day. The patient showed significant clinical improvement. Serial CSF tNGS before and after therapy showed synchronous clearance of three viruses with restored BBB integrity and reduced serum HBV DNA, confirming transient passive HBV entry during HSV-2-induced barrier disruption and creating a false polymicrobial picture. These findings highlight serial tNGS as a valuable tool for validating etiological hypotheses and guiding precision therapy in complex CNS infections.

papers.title: Gut microbiome depletion aggravates glial-mediated Alzheimer's disease pathology through inflammatory, metabolic, and proteostatic dysregulation.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by chronic neuroinflammation, metabolic dysfunction, and impaired proteostasis. Emerging evidence suggests that the gut microbiome influences brain function through the gut-brain axis; however, the mechanisms by which this communication affects AD pathology remain poorly understood. In this study, we used humanized Drosophila AD models expressing human AD-related transgenes in glial cells to investigate how glial AD pathology influences the gut microbiome and how microbiome depletion affects behavior and disease progression. Our findings revealed significant alterations in the abundance of several gut microbial taxa, including Lactobacillus, Acetobacter, Enterococcus, Enterobacter, Pseudomonas, Leuconostoc, Providencia, and Gluconobacter, suggesting a potential interaction between the gut microbiome and AD progression. To further define the role of the gut microbiome in AD progression, we treated Drosophila with antibiotics to achieve substantial microbiome depletion (SMD) and evaluated the resulting behavioral, physiological, and molecular changes. Compared with conventional controls, flies with SMD exhibited enhanced inflammatory signaling and cell death, impaired autophagy, lipid dysregulation, and increased accumulation of amyloid β-42 (aβ42) and phospho-tau (pTau), with the extent of these changes varying among the different humanized AD models. These molecular alterations further exacerbated sleepcircadian disruption, altered locomotor performance, and worsened learning and memory deficits. Furthermore, we demonstrated a link between enhanced neuroinflammation and the accumulation of aβ42, pTau, and amyloid precursor protein (APP) proteins. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that gut microbiome depletion aggravates glial-mediated AD pathology through the coordinated disruption of inflammatory, metabolic, and proteostatic pathways, ultimately leading to behavioral dysfunction. These results identify the gut microbiome as a critical regulator of glial homeostasis and provide new insights into its contribution to the progression of neurodegenerative disorders.
