papers.title: URBANOME: an exposome-based framework linking urban interventions to molecular, health, and policy-relevant outcomes.
papers.abstract: Urban environments expose residents to multiple simultaneous stressors that often act synergistically (e.g., air pollution and extreme heat amplifying cardiovascular and respiratory risks), contributing to a substantial public health burden. Environmental factors account for an estimated 13% of all deaths in the European Union, with ambient air pollution alone responsible for approximately 400,000 premature deaths per year. Most of this burden is mediated through chronic non-communicable diseases, including cardiovascular disease, stroke, cancer, respiratory disease, and mental health outcomes. Because these conditions are shaped by interacting environmental, social, and lifestyle determinants, traditional single-hazard approaches are insufficient, motivating adoption of an exposome paradigm. This paper presents the URBANOME methodological framework, an integrated exposome-based architecture for evaluating urban interventions across external exposures, internal biological responses, functional health outcomes, and policy-relevant indicators, and reports illustrative pilot findings from its first multi-site implementation. In a four-year Horizon 2020 study across nine European cities (Aarhus, Aberdeen, Athens, Ljubljana, Madrid, Milan, Montpellier, Stuttgart, and Thessaloniki), URBANOME implemented an integrated exposome framework through Urban Living Labs (ULLs). Co-created interventions (combining active mobility, urban greening, and traffic calming) were evaluated using a before-after design. Methods included ambient and personal exposure monitoring (wearable sensors, smartphone applications), agent-based population exposure modeling, validated health and well-being questionnaires, objective clinical measures (spirometry, blood pressure, heart rate variability), and multi-omics analyses (untargeted metabolomics and transcriptomics) on biological samples. A cost-benefit analysis quantified the economic return of interventions. The framework was successfully implemented across the nine ULLs, although intervention type, comparator availability, sample size, and follow-up duration varied by site (Table 1). Across paired participants, self-reported air-pollution annoyance and sleep-related breathing problems decreased between baseline and follow-up assessments, and pollution-related differences in forced vital capacity (FVC) were attenuated in higher-exposure neighbourhoods. In an exploratory pilot omics sub-cohort with paired pre/post samples, a four-metabolite panel (L-tyrosine, ascorbic acid, choline, coenzyme Q10) showed apparent perfect internal separation of pre- and post-intervention samples (apparent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, AUROC ≈ 1.0); given the small sample size and absence of an independent held-out validation set, this result is preliminary and likely overoptimistic, and must be interpreted as a hypothesis-generating finding requiring external validation. Exploratory exposome-lifestyle analyses suggested that co-exposure to poor diet and higher pollution was associated with greater oxidative-stress-related metabolic signals, while combined healthy environments and lifestyles were associated with anti-inflammatory metabolite profiles. An exploratory cost-benefit analysis, based on value-transfer assumptions and standard health-economic unit costs, estimated benefit-cost ratios in the range of approximately €19-€143 per €1 invested across heterogeneous interventions; this range reflects substantial between-site variability and the assumptions detailed in the Methods, and should be interpreted as illustrative rather than as a precise return-on-investment estimate. This paper presents the URBANOME exposome-based evaluation framework and reports illustrative pilot findings from its multi-site implementation. The framework is feasible to deploy across heterogeneous European urban contexts and links external exposure assessment, internal biological profiling, functional health outcomes, and economic appraisal within a single architecture. Observed pre/post changes in self-reported, functional, and molecular endpoints are consistent with potentially beneficial responses to bundled urban interventions, but should be considered preliminary given the heterogeneous before-after design, variable comparator availability, small omics sub-cohorts, and short follow-up. External validation of the candidate biomarker panel and replication in independent settings are required before the framework's outputs can support firm conclusions about intervention effectiveness or cost-effectiveness.

papers.title: Cross-species multi-omics integration reveals lung alterations in acute kidney injury across mouse, pig, and human airway organoid models.
papers.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is frequently associated with the development of distant acute lung injury (ALI); however, its broader clinical impact and the underlying temporal molecular mechanisms remain incompletely characterized. We used aggregate deidentified Epic Cosmos data to describe all-cause mortality and hospital length of stay (LOS) in an AKI cohort (13,815,092 patients; 2016-2025) and a subgroup with subsequent lung injury (AKI-lung). Mechanistically, we integrated matched RNA-seq and proteomics from a hyper-acute pig model (4 h reperfusion), an established mouse model (24 h reperfusion), and primary lung organoids exposed to mtDAMP-conditioned media, using MOFA+, PROGENy, decoupleR/CollecTRI, and DIABLO. Candidates were validated in primary human donor lungs obtained from LifeLink, separated into Control (< 1.3 mg/dL, n = 5) and AKI (≥ 1.3 mg/dL, n = 5) groups based on the highest blood creatinine level measured in hospital. The AKI-lung subgroup had higher observed mortality than the overall AKI cohort (36.67% vs. 25.45%, p < 0.001). Mean hospital LOS was 11.3 versus 6.9 days in the reported AKI-lung and AKI alone queries, respectively (unadjusted p < 0.001). Multi-omics analyses cross-species indicated a temporal shift in proteogenomic coupling. In the hyper-acute pig model, we observed a largely post-translational response, including ciliary breakdown and metabolic changes. The established mouse model showed a coordinated transcriptional inflammatory response (r = 0.316), characterized by PI3K/Akt pathway activation and downregulation of vascular and immune regulators (Aplnr, Cd74). Human lung organoids exhibited transcriptional downregulation of tissue remodeling genes and persistent ATF6/ATF4-associated ER stress, consistent with a reparative phase under proteostatic strain. Unsupervised MOFA+ revealed conserved cross-species axes (Factors 6 and 7) linked to vascular repair and hemostasis. Upstream regulon analysis identified the endothelial integrity regulators, including FOXF1. Most importantly, targeted validation in primary human donor lungs confirmed a statistically significant, selective down-regulation of the core circadian regulator circadian locomotor output cycles kaput (CLOCK) transcript (p < 0.05). Aggregate clinical findings suggest an association between lung injury following AKI and worse outcome. Kidney-Lung crosstalk initiates as hyper-acute post-translational microvascular breakdown in swine and rapidly transitions into localized uncoupling of cell-autonomous pulmonary circadian machinery (CLOCK) in clinical human AKI, offering human-validated targets to intercept distant organ failure.
